Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q3 # Executive summary ## Silver: prices will remain strong until 2015 Although the ebb and flow in ETF holdings are no longer providing a demonstrable guide to investors’ desire to buy, our tabulations show that a fundamental surplus of 5,500-6,000 t/y is being generated without putting any immense downward pressure on silver’s price. This latent demand will hold until monetary policy is tightened in 2015. Silver will then fall to $15/oz. - After bouncing back in 2010, fabrication demand has slipped once again in 2011-12. It is forecast to grow at 3-3.5% p.a. in 2013-15 but weaker coinage will be a drag beyond then. - Subject to financing being available, project development would largely be unencumbered at today’s prices. However, mine supply will be curtailed in 2016-17 once prices have fallen. - Even though fabrication demand will struggle to grow in 2016-17 as coinage offtake falls, the price-induced curtailments will rein in mine supply by more and cut the market’s surplus to around 3,000 tonnes in 2017. The stock-to-consumption ratio will then be 2.5-2.6 years. Investors are keeping silver’s price elevated in real terms

CRU International Limited confidential Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q3 Executive Summary 2 ## Other precious metal markets ### Gold The gold market is expected to remain in fundamental surplus over the next five years. After peaking in 2013, the surplus may then decline during the 2014-17 period. - The world’s gold supplies were largely unchanged in the first half of 2012 as a marginal rise in primary gold supply was largely offset by the fall in supply generated by gold recycling programmes. - Central banks continue to diversify their foreign exchange reserves into gold but their interest has started to wane. - Fabrication demand, jewellery in particular, remains weak but is set to improve in later years on the back of lower prices and rising incomes in many key developing countries. ### Platinum The platinum market surplus is shrinking fast as troubles with supply deepen. The return to a nearly balanced market is now expected in 2014 but it is unlikely that the fundamental balance will shift into deficit at any point in our forecast period. - The decline in platinum mine production is expected to continue in 2013 based in part on the decisions made in 2012 to curtail or defer expansion plans. - Demand from global car manufacturers is expected to strengthen next year thanks to the introduction of Euro VI emissions rules for new vehicles coming into effect on January 1st 2013. - During 2014-17,

Should you have any problems with using the CRUOnline website, please contact the helpdesk on Tel +44 20 7903 2113 (09.00–18.00 UK time), or e-mail:- support.cruonline@crugroup.com The following lists the different statistics and downloads that are available to you as a _Precious Metals Quarterly_ subscriber: #### **Quarterly Report** - Pdf version of this report - Separate excel workbooks with our forecast tables for gold, silver, platinum and - palladium (supply-demand balances, consumption by country and use, mine production by country and operation, scrap generation, more) #### **Market Statistics** (all in excel) - COTF futures and options contracts - Gold, silver, platinum and palladium ETF holdings - Prices (precious metals prices and other key indicators) - Statistics (summarised data on prices, exchanges, exchange rates, local prices etc) - Gold, silver, platinum and palladium bullion imports by country - Central Bank gold reserves - UK jewellery hallmarkings - Bombay gold prices and premia - LBMA monthly clearing turnover statistics for gold and silver - Lease rates for gold and silver - US Eagle coin sales CRU International Limited

## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), GTIS trade statistics, and company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of these data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
